    Hands-on

    These steps were checked in QGIS 4.0 (QGIS 3.34 and later are nearly identical). Save a new project in its own folder first; raster results are written there.

    Callout

    If QGIS asks you to choose a transformation

    When layers in latitude and longitude (EPSG:4326) are drawn in a project in UTM (EPSG:26916), QGIS may open a window that begins “Multiple operations are possible for converting coordinates”. For this county any of the options is accurate to a few meters: keep the first (highlighted) one and click OK.

    Part 1: Load the rasters from the web

    1. Layer > Add Layer > Add Raster Layer. Source Type: Protocol: HTTP(S), cloud, etc. Type: HTTP/HTTPS/FTP. URI: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/Foundations/main/data/tippecanoe_dem.tif. Click Add.
    2. Repeat with https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/Foundations/main/data/tippecanoe_landcover_2021.tif.
    3. Load the tracts as a vector layer: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/Foundations/main/data/tippecanoe_tracts_acs.geojson.

    Check: the land cover appears in the official NLCD colors (the file carries its color table), and the elevation in gray, dark in the Wabash valley. Right-click the elevation layer > Properties > Information: CRS EPSG:26916, pixel size 30 by 30.

    Part 2: Land below 170 m (Raster Calculator)

    1. Raster > Raster Calculator.
    2. In Raster Bands, double-click tippecanoe_dem@1 to insert it, then type < 170 so the expression reads "tippecanoe_dem@1" < 170.
    3. Output layer: click … and save as low.tif in your project folder (or tick Create on-the-fly raster to skip saving). OK stays gray until an output is set.
    4. Click OK.

    The result has 1 where the comparison is true and 0 where it is false.

    Check: in the Processing Toolbox, run Raster layer unique values report on low. Value 1 covers 96,559 cells, about 86.9 km².

    Part 3: Group the land cover (Reclassify by table)

    1. Processing Toolbox: Reclassify by table. Raster layer: tippecanoe_landcover_2021.
    2. Reclassification table: click … and add eight rows (Add Row) with Minimum, Maximum and Value as in the table above: 11, 12, 1 / 21, 24, 2 / 31, 31, 3 / 41, 43, 3 / 52, 52, 3 / 71, 71, 3 / 81, 82, 4 / 90, 95, 5. Click the back arrow to return.
    3. Open Advanced Parameters. Range boundaries: min <= value <= max (the default min < value <= max would skip codes 11, 21, 31 and so on). Tick Use NoData when no range matches value. Output data type: Byte.
    4. Save the output as landcover_groups.tif and click Run.

    Check: the unique values report on landcover_groups shows five values: 1 about 10.8 km², 2 about 196.8 km², 3 about 167.1 km², 4 about 904.0 km², 5 about 23.4 km². If group 1 or 2 is much smaller, check the range boundaries.

    Part 4: Developed land below 170 m

    1. Raster > Raster Calculator again, with the expression ("low@1" = 1) AND ("landcover_groups@1" = 2), saved as low_developed.tif.
    2. Run the unique values report on it.

    Check: value 1 covers about 10.7 km², about 5% of the county’s 196.8 km² of developed land.

    Part 5: Mean elevation per tract (Zonal statistics)

    1. Reproject the tracts to the rasters’ CRS: Vector > Data Management Tools > Reproject Layer, target EPSG:26916, and rename the result tracts_utm.
    2. Processing Toolbox: Zonal statistics (in the Raster analysis group). Input layer: tracts_utm. Raster layer: tippecanoe_dem. Output column prefix: elev_. Statistics to calculate: tick Mean, Minimum and Maximum. Run.

    Check: the new layer has elev_mean, elev_min and elev_max. Census Tract 1 has a mean of about 165.6 m, one of the lowest, close to the river.

    Part 6: Percent developed per tract (Zonal histogram)

    1. Processing Toolbox: Zonal histogram. Raster layer: landcover_groups. Vector layer containing zones: the output of Part 5 (or tracts_utm). Leave the prefix as HISTO_. Run.

    1. The output has one column per group: HISTO_1 to HISTO_5 (cell counts), plus HISTO_NODATA.

    2. In its attribute table, open the Field Calculator and create pct_developed, Decimal Number (real):

      "HISTO_2" / ("HISTO_1" + "HISTO_2" + "HISTO_3" + "HISTO_4" + "HISTO_5") * 100

    Check: the lowest value is Census Tract 110 at about 4.8%; the median is about 82%, and several downtown tracts are 100%.

    Part 7: Map it

    Style the result with Graduated symbology on pct_developed, Natural Breaks (Jenks), 5 classes, a sequential ramp such as Reds.

    Compare it with a map of population density (total_pop divided by the tract area): the patterns are very similar. That is why land cover is useful for placing people within tracts, the idea behind dasymetric estimation. The Python version (notebook 2b) carries out the dasymetric estimate.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Which resampling?

    You need to combine a 10 m land cover raster with a 30 m elevation raster. Which raster would you resample, to what cell size, and with which method? (In QGIS: Raster > Projections > Warp (Reproject) has a Resampling method option.)

    Resample the land cover to 30 m (the coarser resolution), with nearest neighbor (Nearest Neighbour in the Warp dialog), because it holds categories: bilinear would average codes into classes that do not exist. Resampling the elevation to 10 m would create a finer grid without adding information.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: A different threshold

    Repeat Parts 2 and 4 with 175 m. How much developed land lies below it? Is the answer sensitive to the threshold?

    "tippecanoe_dem@1" < 175, then the AND step: about 15.3 km² (compared with 10.7 km² below 170 m). Five meters of threshold add about 40%, so the result is quite sensitive, which is one more reason to use a real flood map for decisions.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Mean or count?

    For each tract you want (a) its average elevation, (b) its share of forest, and (c) its most common land cover class. Which QGIS tool and statistic gives each?

    1. Zonal statistics, Mean, on the elevation raster. (b) Zonal histogram on the land cover (or the groups), then forest cells divided by all cells in the Field Calculator. (c) Zonal statistics, Majority, on the land cover raster. Never the Mean of land cover codes.
    Key Points
    • Rasters combined cell by cell must share CRS, cell size and extent; resample categories with nearest neighbor
    • The Raster Calculator makes comparisons and combines conditions (AND, OR); results are 1 and 0
    • Reclassify by table groups codes; set the range boundaries to min <= value <= max for whole-number codes
    • Zonal statistics summarize measurements per polygon; Zonal histogram counts categories per polygon
    • Check results with the unique values report: cells times 900 m² gives areas

    Content from Automating Repeated Steps in Python

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 70 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • When is it worth automating a processing workflow?
    • How do I turn a sequence of steps into a function, and run it for many inputs?
    • How do I make an automated workflow trustworthy?

    Objectives

    • Write a function with parameters and defaults that packages a geoprocessing workflow
    • Test the function against a known result before using it on new inputs
    • Use loops and groupby to run a workflow for many distances, layers or counties, and collect the results
    • Check inputs, report what each run did, and keep one failure from stopping a long loop

    When to automate

    The Geoprocessing episode answered one question: how many people in Lafayette and West Lafayette live within 1 mile of a supermarket? Real projects rarely stop at one answer. A reviewer asks about half a mile; a partner asks about parks; next year’s ACS data arrives; a colleague wants the same numbers for another county. Each request means running the same steps again with one input changed.

    Doing that by hand is slow, but the bigger problem is mistakes: a step skipped, an old layer selected in a drop-down list, a distance typed as 1690 instead of 1609. Automation means writing the steps down once, in a form the computer can repeat exactly, with the parts that change made into parameters.

    A useful rule of thumb: the first time, do it by hand and understand it; the second time, notice you are repeating yourself; the third time, automate. A one-off task is often not worth automating, but it is still worth recording (see the Introduction).

    Levels of automation

    Level Python QGIS Good for
    Record The notebook itself Processing > History; a tool’s Advanced > Copy as Python Command Seeing exactly what was run, with which settings
    Repeat one tool A for loop around one function call Run as Batch Process (one row per run) The same tool on many inputs or settings
    Package several steps A function with parameters A model in the Model Designer A workflow you will run again with different inputs
    Run for every feature A loop over groupby groups or rows The Iterate button (green arrows) next to an input layer One output per county, per city, per study area
    Run without you A script run on a schedule or a server qgis_process on the command line Regular updates, very large jobs

    This episode covers the first four. The two tools mirror each other closely: a Python function and a QGIS model are both “these steps, with these inputs”; a loop and a batch run are both “again, for each of these”.

    Writing steps you can trust

    Automated steps run without anyone watching, so they need habits that manual work can do without:

    • Test on a known answer. Before running a function or model on new inputs, run it on a case you have already worked out by hand. Here: 77,473 people within 1 mile of a supermarket, from the Geoprocessing episode. If it does not match, find out why before going further.
    • Make the parameters explicit. Every value that might change (a distance, a layer, a column) becomes a parameter with a clear name and, if there is a usual value, a default. Values that should not change (the projected CRS, the number of buffer segments) stay inside.
    • Check inputs and fail loudly. A workflow that silently buffers in degrees is worse than one that stops with a message. Check the things that commonly go wrong (CRS, expected columns, row counts) at the start, or make the workflow fix them itself (the QGIS model reprojects every input).
    • Report what happened. Print or log the number of rows read, codes replaced, features joined and features written. These counts are your evidence that each run worked.
    • Never overwrite inputs. Write results to new layers or files with systematic names (near_400.gpkg, near_800.gpkg), so a rerun cannot destroy the raw data or an earlier result.
    • Keep one failure from stopping everything, but do not hide it. When looping over 92 counties, catch an error for one county, record it and move on, then read the list of failures at the end.

    Summaries over many units

    Running the same summary for every county raises a classic question: how do you combine tract values into a county value? Add up counts first, then compute rates from the sums (households without a car divided by all households). Averaging tract percentages gives a small rural tract the same weight as a large urban one and answers a different question. Medians cannot be added up at all: a county median income must come from the county-level ACS table, not from the tract medians.

    Callout

    The same automation in QGIS

    The Automating Repeated Steps in QGIS episode builds the same workflow as a Model Designer model and runs it as a batch, with the same results: 6.9%, 23.2% and 67.8% of residents within 400 m, 800 m and 1 mile of a supermarket.

    The workflow in code

    The function, the test and the loop at the heart of notebook 4a:

    PYTHON 

    def pop_within(facilities, distance, tracts=tracts, boundary=city, column="total_pop"):
    """People inside `boundary` within `distance` meters of `facilities` (areal weighting)."""
    t = tracts.copy()
    t["tract_m2"] = t.area
    in_boundary = gpd.clip(t, boundary)
    zone = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[facilities.buffer(distance).union_all()], crs=t.crs)
    near = gpd.overlay(in_boundary, zone, how="intersection")
    people_near = (near.area / near["tract_m2"] * near[column]).sum()
    people_all = (in_boundary.area / in_boundary["tract_m2"] * in_boundary[column]).sum()
    return round(people_near), round(people_all), round(people_near / people_all * 100, 1)

assert pop_within(supermarkets, 1609)[0] == 77473          # the Geoprocessing episode's answer

rows = []
for d in [400, 800, 1609, 3218]:
    near, total, share = pop_within(supermarkets, d)
    rows.append({"distance_m": d, "people_within": near, "share_pct": share})
pd.DataFrame(rows)

    Notebook 4b wraps the Census cleaning of the Cleaning episode in a clean_acs() function, runs it on all 1,696 Indiana tracts, and summarizes all 92 counties with a loop (and with groupby().apply()).

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Parameter or not?

    You are turning the park access analysis into a function. Which of these should be parameters, which should have defaults, and which should stay fixed inside the function?

    1. The parks layer
    2. The walking distance (800 m)
    3. The projected CRS (EPSG:26916)
    4. The population column (total_pop)
    5. The number of segments used to draw buffer circles
    1. A parameter without a default: the function is about some set of parks or facilities.
    2. A parameter with a default of 800: the usual case, easy to change for a sensitivity test.
    3. Fixed (or checked): it is a technical requirement, not a choice the user should make each time. For another state you would change it once, or make the function choose a suitable CRS.
    4. A parameter with a default of total_pop, so the same function can count children or households.
    5. Fixed: it affects the result only slightly and should be the same in every run so results are comparable.
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: The average of percentages

    A loop over Indiana’s counties computes each county’s share of households without a car as the mean of its tracts’ pct_no_vehicle. For Tippecanoe County this gives 10.3%, but notebook 4b reports 9.7%. Which is right, and why do they differ?

    9.7% is the share of the county’s households: the sum of households without a car divided by the sum of households. The mean of 42 tract percentages (10.3%) gives every tract the same weight, so small tracts near campus with very high shares pull it up. It answers “what is the typical tract like?”, not “what share of the county’s households have no car?”. Add counts first, then divide.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: A silent failure

    A colleague’s loop over 92 counties uses try: ... except: pass so that “nothing stops the loop”. The output table has 88 rows and no error appeared. What went wrong with the design, and how would you change it?

    except: pass hides every error, so four counties failed without a trace. Catch the error, but record it: print the county and the message, or append it to a list of failures, and check the count at the end (assert len(table) == 92, or report how many failed). Then fix the cause and rerun.

    Key Points
    • Automate work you will repeat; record work you will not
    • A function packages steps; parameters are the parts that change, defaults the usual values
    • Test on a known answer, check inputs, and report counts so every run leaves evidence
    • Loops (or groupby) run the same workflow for many inputs and collect the results in one table
    • Combine units by adding counts first, then computing rates
    • Catch errors in long loops, but record them and check the totals at the end

    Notebooks

    Notebook What you will do
    4a. Functions and Loops Turn the Geoprocessing episode’s areal weighting into a function, test it, and loop over distances and facility layers
    4b. Many Counties Clean the ACS table for all of Indiana with one function, explain the rows that do not join, summarize 92 counties and save a map per county

    Content from Automating Repeated Steps in QGIS

    Last updated on 2026-10-25 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 75 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • When is it worth automating a processing workflow?
    • How do I record, repeat and package processing steps in QGIS?
    • How do I make an automated workflow trustworthy?

    Objectives

    • Find and rerun earlier tools with the Processing History
    • Build a model in the Model Designer with inputs, algorithms and outputs
    • Test the model against a known result, then run it as a batch for several distances
    • Reuse the model for other facilities and other population fields

    When to automate

    The Geoprocessing episode answered one question: how many people in Lafayette and West Lafayette live within 1 mile of a supermarket? Real projects rarely stop at one answer. A reviewer asks about half a mile; a partner asks about parks; next year’s ACS data arrives; a colleague wants the same numbers for another county. Each request means running the same steps again with one input changed.

    Doing that by hand is slow, but the bigger problem is mistakes: a step skipped, an old layer selected in a drop-down list, a distance typed as 1690 instead of 1609. Automation means writing the steps down once, in a form the computer can repeat exactly, with the parts that change made into parameters.

    A useful rule of thumb: the first time, do it by hand and understand it; the second time, notice you are repeating yourself; the third time, automate. A one-off task is often not worth automating, but it is still worth recording (see the Introduction).

    Levels of automation

    Level Python QGIS Good for
    Record The notebook itself Processing > History; a tool’s Advanced > Copy as Python Command Seeing exactly what was run, with which settings
    Repeat one tool A for loop around one function call Run as Batch Process (one row per run) The same tool on many inputs or settings
    Package several steps A function with parameters A model in the Model Designer A workflow you will run again with different inputs
    Run for every feature A loop over groupby groups or rows The Iterate button (green arrows) next to an input layer One output per county, per city, per study area
    Run without you A script run on a schedule or a server qgis_process on the command line Regular updates, very large jobs

    This episode covers the first four. The two tools mirror each other closely: a Python function and a QGIS model are both “these steps, with these inputs”; a loop and a batch run are both “again, for each of these”.

    • Make the parameters explicit. Every value that might change (a distance, a layer, a column) becomes a parameter with a clear name and, if there is a usual value, a default. Values that should not change (the projected CRS, the number of buffer segments) stay inside.
    • Check inputs and fail loudly. A workflow that silently buffers in degrees is worse than one that stops with a message. Check the things that commonly go wrong (CRS, expected columns, row counts) at the start, or make the workflow fix them itself (the QGIS model reprojects every input).
    • Report what happened. Print or log the number of rows read, codes replaced, features joined and features written. These counts are your evidence that each run worked.
    • Never overwrite inputs. Write results to new layers or files with systematic names (near_400.gpkg, near_800.gpkg), so a rerun cannot destroy the raw data or an earlier result.
    • Keep one failure from stopping everything, but do not hide it. When looping over 92 counties, catch an error for one county, record it and move on, then read the list of failures at the end.

    Running the same summary for every county raises a classic question: how do you combine tract values into a county value? Add up counts first, then compute rates from the sums (households without a car divided by all households). Averaging tract percentages gives a small rural tract the same weight as a large urban one and answers a different question. Medians cannot be added up at all: a county median income must come from the county-level ACS table, not from the tract medians.

    Callout

    The same automation in Python

    The Automating Repeated Steps in Python episode writes the same workflow as a function and runs it in a loop, with the same results. It also cleans the ACS table for all of Indiana and summarizes all 92 counties, a task that shows where code is the better tool.

    Hands-on

    These steps were checked in QGIS 4.0; the Model Designer looks the same in QGIS 3.34 and later. The workflow packaged here is the one from the Geoprocessing in QGIS episode (Parts 2 to 8): reproject, store tract areas, buffer and dissolve, clip, intersect and split the population by area.

    Part 1: Load the inputs

    Add these four layers with Layer > Add Layer > Add Vector Layer, Protocol: HTTP(S), cloud, etc., Type: HTTP/HTTPS/FTP:

    Layer File
    Grocery stores grocery_stores.geojson
    City limits study_area.geojson
    Tracts with ACS data tippecanoe_tracts_acs.geojson
    Parks tippecanoe_parks.geojson

    Web addresses to copy:

    • Grocery stores: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/CaseStudies/main/data/grocery_stores.geojson
    • City limits: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/CaseStudies/main/data/study_area.geojson
    • Tracts with ACS data: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/Foundations/main/data/tippecanoe_tracts_acs.geojson
    • Parks: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/Foundations/main/data/tippecanoe_parks.geojson

    Then run Extract by attribute on grocery_stores (store_type = Supermarket) and rename the result supermarkets (17 points).

    Part 2: The Processing History

    Open Processing > History. Every tool you have run is listed with its exact settings, newest first, grouped by date. Double-click the Extract by attribute entry: the tool opens again with the same settings, ready to run with a change. Each tool dialog also has Advanced > Copy as Python Command, which copies the step as one line of PyQGIS code. Together they mean nothing you run in the Processing Toolbox is ever lost; the History is the first place to look when you need to write up your methods.

    Part 3: Build a model

    The Model Designer chains tools into a new tool of your own. Open it with Processing > Model Designer.

    1. In Model Properties (left), set Name Population within distance and Group SpatialTurn.

    2. Add the inputs from the Inputs tab by dragging each onto the canvas (or double-clicking it):

      Input type Description Settings
      Vector Features Facilities (points or polygons) Geometry type: any
      Number Distance (meters) Number type: Float, default 1609
      Vector Features Tracts with a population field Geometry type: polygon
      Field Population field Parent layer: Tracts; field type: Numeric; default total_pop
      Vector Features Boundary (for example city limits) Geometry type: polygon

    3. Add the algorithms from the Toolbox tab, in this order. In each dialog, choose the input from the drop-down list (the small button next to a parameter switches between a fixed value, a model input and an algorithm output):

      Algorithm Description Settings
      Reproject layer Reproject facilities Input: the Facilities input; Target CRS: EPSG:26916
      Reproject layer Reproject tracts Input: Tracts; EPSG:26916
      Reproject layer Reproject boundary Input: Boundary; EPSG:26916
      Field calculator Store tract area Input: output of Reproject tracts; field tract_m2, Decimal; formula area($geometry)
      Buffer Buffer and dissolve Input: output of Reproject facilities; Distance: the Distance input; Segments 16; Dissolve result ticked
      Clip Clip tracts to boundary Input: output of Store tract area; Overlay: output of Reproject boundary
      Field calculator Population in boundary Input: output of Clip; field pop_in_boundary, Decimal; formula area($geometry) / "tract_m2" * attribute(@populationfield); type a name in its output box to make it a model output: Population in boundary
      Intersection Intersect with buffer Input: output of Population in boundary; Overlay: output of Buffer and dissolve
      Field calculator Population near facilities Input: output of Intersect; field pop_near, Decimal; formula area($geometry) / "tract_m2" * attribute(@populationfield); model output Population near facilities

      Inside a model every input is also a variable, named after its description without spaces, punctuation or capitals: the Population field input is @populationfield. attribute() reads the field with that name, which is what lets the same model count residents, children or households.

    4. Save the model (Model > Save Model). It now appears in the Processing Toolbox under Models.

    If you are short of time, or want to compare with your own, download the finished model from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/DataProcessing/main/data/population_within_distance.model3 (save the page as a file), then in the Processing Toolbox click the Models button (three gears) > Add Model to Toolbox.

    Callout

    Why does the model reproject everything?

    The Geoprocessing episode showed what happens when a layer in degrees is buffered by 1,609: the “buffer” covers the whole Earth. Instead of hoping every user remembers to reproject first, the model does it itself. This is the QGIS version of “check inputs and fail loudly”: make the common mistake impossible.

    Part 4: Test the model on a known answer

    1. Run the model from the Processing Toolbox (Models > SpatialTurn > Population within distance) with Facilities supermarkets, Distance 1609, Tracts tippecanoe_tracts_acs, Population field total_pop and Boundary study_area. Leave both outputs as temporary layers.

    2. Select all features of Population near facilities and look at the Statistics panel for pop_near: the sum is 77,473. For Population in boundary, the sum of pop_in_boundary is 114,345.

    These are exactly the Geoprocessing episode’s numbers (67.8%). Only now is the model ready for new questions.

    Part 5: Run it as a batch

    1. Right-click the model in the Toolbox and choose Execute as Batch Process (or click Run as Batch Process in its dialog).

    2. Click the green + to make three rows. In the first row set the four layers and the field; then use Autofill… > Fill Down in each of those columns to copy them to the other rows.

    3. Type the distances 400, 800 and 1609.

    4. In each output column, type a layer name (near_400, near_800, near_1609; city_400 and so on for the other output) and choose Create Temporary Layer from its … menu, or save to files instead (Save to File…; its Fill with parameter values option builds the names from the Distance column). Tick Load layers on completion, then Run.

    Check: the sums of pop_near are about 7,900 (400 m), 26,600 (800 m) and 77,500 (1 mile): 6.9%, 23.2% and 67.8% of the 114,345 residents.

    Part 6: Reuse the model

    Run the model again, changing only the inputs:

    • Facilities tippecanoe_parks, Distance 800: about 81,800 residents, 71.5%, live within 800 m of a park (polygons are buffered from their edges).
    • Facilities supermarkets, Distance 1609, Population field pop_under18: about 14,800 of 19,540 children, 75.7%.

    Two new answers, with no new geoprocessing by hand.

    Callout

    One output per feature: the Iterate button

    Many Processing tools show a small green Iterate over this layer button (two curved arrows) next to an input layer. With it ticked, the tool runs once for every feature of that layer and writes a separate output for each: for example, Clip tracts with a counties layer, iterating over the counties, gives one tract layer per county. Select a few features first (and tick Selected features only) to keep the number of outputs small.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Batch, model or iterate?

    Which QGIS tool would you use?

    1. Reproject twelve layers to EPSG:26916.
    2. Every month, rerun a five-step workflow on a new file of reported potholes.
    3. Make one map layer of tracts for each of the 92 Indiana counties.
    1. Batch processing of Reproject Layer: one tool, twelve rows (Autofill fills the CRS down).
    2. A model: several steps in a fixed order, with the new file as an input. Save it so next month’s run takes one dialog.
    3. Iterate over this layer on the counties input of Clip (or Extract by Location): one output per feature.
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Parameter or not?

    You are turning the park access analysis into a model. Which of these should be model inputs, and which should be fixed inside the model? The parks layer; the walking distance; the projected CRS; the population field; the number of buffer segments.

    The parks layer, the distance (default 800) and the population field (default total_pop) are inputs: they are the things you will change. The CRS and the number of segments stay fixed inside, so every run is done the same way and results stay comparable.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: A suspicious result

    A classmate’s version of the model reports that 100% of residents live within 800 m of a supermarket. Their model has no Reproject steps, and their supermarkets layer is in EPSG:4326. What happened?

    Without reprojection, Buffer uses the layer’s units: 800 degrees, which covers the whole planet, so every tract is “near”. The fix is the one in this model: reproject inside the model (or check the CRS and stop). Testing the model on the known 1-mile answer first would have caught the problem before any new results were reported.

    Key Points
    • Automate work you will repeat; record work you will not (Processing > History)
    • A model packages several tools; its inputs are the parts that change
    • Test a model on a known answer before using it on new questions
    • Run as Batch Process repeats a tool or model with different settings, one row per run
    • Iterate over this layer runs a tool once per feature
    • Make common mistakes impossible inside the model, for example by reprojecting every input
